name: Worms Synagogue
bio: Founded in 1034 and repeatedly rebuilt, the synagogue at Worms is one of the oldest and most important surviving sites of medieval Ashkenazi Jewish life. The present building is a careful postwar reconstruction on the historic site.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Old New Synagogue
bio: Completed in the late thirteenth century, Prague's Old New Synagogue is among Europe's oldest surviving synagogues still used for worship and a central monument of Ashkenazi Jewish history.
image_credit: BrokenSphere, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

name: Remuh Synagogue
bio: The Remuh Synagogue is the smallest historic synagogue in Kraków's Kazimierz district. Built in the sixteenth century, it remains associated with the adjacent Jewish cemetery and continues to serve worshippers.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons image; attribution and licence are available on the file page.

name: Ibn Danan Synagogue
bio: A seventeenth-century synagogue in the Fes el-Jdid mellah, Ibn Danan preserves the architecture and devotional world of Morocco's historic Jewish community.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Great Synagogue of Vilna
bio: For centuries the Great Synagogue stood at the heart of Vilna's famed Shulhoyf. Damaged during the Holocaust, its remains were demolished under Soviet rule; archaeological work has since recovered important parts of the complex.
image_credit: Model photograph from Wikimedia Commons; attribution and licence are available on the file page.

name: Portuguese Synagogue of Amsterdam
bio: Inaugurated in 1675, Amsterdam's monumental Portuguese Synagogue became a defining institution of the prosperous Sephardi community and remains in religious use.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Great Synagogue of London
bio: The historic central synagogue of London, destroyed during the Blitz in 1941.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Hurva Synagogue
bio: A defining landmark of Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter. Founded in 1700, destroyed and rebuilt more than once, the Hurva became a symbol of the destruction and renewal of Jewish communal life in the Old City.
image_credit: PikiWiki Israel image hosted by Wikimedia Commons.

name: Bevis Marks Synagogue
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Great Synagogue of Gibraltar
bio: Founded in 1724, Sha'ar Hashamayim is Gibraltar's oldest synagogue and the historic centre of one of the western Mediterranean's most enduring Sephardi communities.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Board of Deputies of British Jews
bio: Founded in 1760, the Board of Deputies developed into the principal representative body of British Jewry, engaging government and public institutions on communal concerns.
hebrew_name: ועד שליחי הקהילות של יהודי בריטניה
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Touro Synagogue
bio: Dedicated in 1763, Touro Synagogue in Newport is the oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States and a landmark in the history of American religious liberty.
image_credit: Kenneth C. Zirkel, Wikimedia Commons.

name: Yeshivat Volozhin
bio: A
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Mir Yeshiva
bio: Mir Yeshiva, founded in 1815 in Mir, Belarus, grew into one of the largest and most famous Lithuanian yeshivas. Under Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Finkel and others, it became a powerhouse of Torah study. During WWII, the entire yeshiva escaped via Siberia and Japan to Shanghai, China, making it the only European yeshiva to survive intact. After the war it was reestablished in Jerusalem and Brooklyn, becoming the largest yeshiva in the world.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Etz Chaim Yeshiva
bio: Founded in Jerusalem's Old City in 1841, Etz Chaim became a foundational institution of the Old Yishuv and later occupied its well-known Jaffa Road complex near Mahane Yehuda.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons image; attribution and licence are available on the file page.

name: B'nai B'rith International
bio: Founded by German-Jewish immigrants in New York in 1843, B'nai B'rith became an international Jewish service, welfare and advocacy organisation.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Dohány Street Synagogue
bio: The monumental Dohány Street Synagogue is a principal landmark of Hungarian Jewry and one of the world's largest synagogue buildings. Its complex now also commemorates victims of the Holocaust.
image_credit: Adam Jones, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

name: Alliance Israélite Universelle
bio: Established in Paris in 1860, the Alliance Israélite Universelle created an influential international network of Jewish schools and campaigned for Jewish civil and human rights.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Kelm Talmud Torah Yeshiva
bio: The Kelm Talmud Torah (often simply called 'Kelm') was a Lithuanian yeshiva established in 1866 in Kelm, Lithuania. It became one of the central institutions of the Musar Movement under Rabbi Simcha Zissel Ziv, known as the 'Saba of Kelm.' It emphasized strict order, discipline, and ethical self-mastery. The yeshiva produced many of the leading figures of the Musar and Lithuanian Torah world. It was tragically destroyed during the Holocaust in 1941 when its students and townspeople were massacred.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: New Synagogue, Berlin
bio: Inaugurated in 1866, Berlin's New Synagogue was the city's great Moorish Revival synagogue. Its surviving frontage and dome now combine prayer space, museum and memorial functions.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Spanish Synagogue of Prague
bio: Built in 1868 on the site of Prague's Old School, the Spanish Synagogue is celebrated for its Moorish Revival design and richly ornamented interior. It now forms part of the Jewish Museum in Prague.
image_credit: Thomas Ledl, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

name: Radun Yeshiva
bio: The Radun Yeshiva was founded in 1869 in Radun, Belarus, by Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan, known as the Chofetz Chaim. It became famous for its emphasis on ethical conduct and halakhic study. The yeshiva was dispersed during World War I but regrouped later. It was destroyed during the Holocaust, though its legacy continued through students and the Radin Talmud Torah in Israel and the US.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: United Synagogue
bio: Created by an Act of Parliament in 1870, the United Synagogue became Britain's largest Orthodox synagogue umbrella body and a central provider of religious and communal services.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Central Synagogue
bio: Central Synagogue's Moorish Revival building is one of New York City's most recognizable Jewish landmarks and one of the oldest synagogue buildings in continuous use in the city.
hebrew_name: בית הכנסת המרכזי של ניו יורק
image_credit: Elisa Rolle, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

name: Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary
bio: Founded by ר׳ עזריאל הילדסהיימר in 1873, the Berlin Rabbinical Seminary united advanced Torah learning with university scholarship and trained a generation of Orthodox rabbis before Nazi closure in 1938.
image_credit: Historic seminary image from Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Princes Road Synagogue
bio: Consecrated in 1874, Liverpool's Princes Road Synagogue is a richly decorated Moorish Revival landmark created for the city's growing Victorian Jewish community.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Hebrew Union College
bio: Founded in Cincinnati in 1875, Hebrew Union College became the principal American seminary of Reform Judaism and later developed campuses in New York, Los Angeles and Jerusalem.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Telz Yeshiva
bio: Founded in 1875 in Telšiai, Lithuania, Telz Yeshiva became a leading institution of the Mussar movement, emphasizing structured discipline alongside sharp Talmudic analysis. Led by Rabbi Eliezer Gordon and later Rabbi Yosef Leib Bloch, it trained many prominent rabbis. The original yeshiva was destroyed in the Holocaust in 1941, but a branch was reestablished in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1941 by survivors.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Great Synagogue of Florence
bio: Completed in 1882, Florence's monumental copper-domed synagogue expresses the public confidence of Italian Jewry after emancipation and national unification.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Slabodka Yeshiva
bio: Slabodka Yeshiva, founded in the 1880s in the Slabodka suburb of Kaunas, Lithuania, was one of the most influential Lithuanian yeshivas. Under Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel ('the Alter of Slabodka') it emphasized Musar, especially the idea of 'Gadlus HaAdam' (the greatness of man). It produced many leading rabbis and rosh yeshivas of the 20th century. In 1924, part of the yeshiva moved to Hebron, and later relocated to Bnei Brak after the 1929 Hebron massacre.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Lomza Yeshiva
bio: Founded in Łomża in 1883, the yeshiva became an important Musar institution. Its Petah Tikva branch, opened during the interwar period, preserved the name and institutional legacy in the Land of Israel.
image_credit: Israel Zeller / PikiWiki Israel, CC BY 2.5.

name: Jewish Theological Seminary
bio: Founded in 1886, the Jewish Theological Seminary became a central academic and rabbinical institution of Conservative Judaism in North America.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Yeshiva University and RIETS
bio: Rooted in the Etz Chaim yeshiva founded in 1886 and the Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary established in 1897, Yeshiva University became a central institution of Modern Orthodox scholarship and rabbinic education.
hebrew_name: ישיבה יוניברסיטי וישיבת רבינו יצחק אלחנן
image_credit: Beyond My Ken, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

name: Eldridge Street Synagogue
bio: Opened in 1887, the Eldridge Street Synagogue was the first great purpose-built house of worship erected in New York by Eastern European Orthodox Jewish immigrants.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: National Library of Israel
bio: Beginning in Jerusalem in 1892 and later serving the Hebrew University, the National Library of Israel became the national repository for the documentary heritage of Israel and the Jewish people.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Novardok Yeshiva
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Machzikei Hadath - Spitalfields
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Mesivta Rabsa Eitz Chaim D'Slutsk (Slutsk-Kletsk Yeshiva)
bio: The Slutsk-Kletsk Yeshiva was an Orthodox Lithuanian yeshiva founded in 1897 in Slutsk by Rabbi Yaakov Dovid Willovsky (Ridvaz) to combat the influence of the Haskalah. It was led by Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer and later his son-in-law, Rabbi Aharon Kotler, who carried the yeshiva to Kletsk and ultimately reestablished it in America as Beth Medrash Govoha. The yeshiva was renowned for its elite students, intense Talmudic learning, and resilience through war, revolution, and exile.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: World Zionist Organization
bio: Created at the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, the World Zionist Organization provided the international political and institutional framework of the Zionist movement.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Orthodox Union
bio: Founded in 1898, the Orthodox Union became one of the largest Orthodox Jewish organisations in North America, supporting synagogues, education, youth work, advocacy and major kosher-certification operations.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Jewish National Fund
bio: Founded by the Fifth Zionist Congress in 1901, the Jewish National Fund acquired and developed land and later became closely associated with forestry, water and environmental projects in Israel.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: World Mizrachi
bio: Founded in Vilna in 1902, Mizrachi organised Religious Zionism internationally and promoted a programme joining Torah commitment with Jewish national restoration.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Great Synagogue of Rome
bio: Completed after the abolition of Rome's ghetto, the Great Synagogue became the principal house of worship and a prominent architectural symbol of the historic Roman Jewish community.
image_credit: Cats' photos, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

name: Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Berlin
bio: Established in 1904, Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Berlin grew into a major Brooklyn Orthodox yeshiva and rabbinical academy.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Bournemouth Hebrew Congregation
bio: Orthodox synagogue in Bournemouth
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: American Jewish Committee
bio: Established in New York in 1906 amid concern over persecution and pogroms in the Russian Empire, the American Jewish Committee developed into an international Jewish advocacy organisation.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Yeshiva Ohel Torah-Baranovich
bio: Yeshiva Ohel Torah-Baranovich was one of the most influential Lithuanian yeshivot of pre-World War II Eastern Europe. Founded around 1906 in Baranovich by Rabbi Yosef Yoizel Horowitz, the Alter of Novardok, it became famous under the leadership of Rabbi Elchonon Wasserman, a leading disciple of the Chofetz Chaim. The yeshiva combined intense Talmudic analysis with the Novardok mussar tradition and produced many distinguished תלמידי חכמים. It was destroyed during World War II, when Rabbi Elchonon Wasserman and many students were murdered by the Nazis and their collaborators.
image_credit: Photograph by Andrei Dybovskii (2006), served by the Center for Jewish Art.

name: Ponevezh Yeshiva
bio: Founded in Panevėžys in 1908 and re-established in Bnei Brak during the Holocaust era, Ponevezh became one of the leading institutions of the postwar Lithuanian yeshiva world.
image_credit: Dr Avishai Teicher / PikiWiki Israel, Wikimedia Commons.

name: Hadassah
bio: Founded in New York in 1912, Hadassah built a mass women's Zionist organisation whose medical, educational and welfare projects became enduring institutions in Jerusalem and across Israel.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: World Agudath Israel
bio: Founded at Katowice in 1912, World Agudath Israel created an international political and communal framework for Orthodox communities that opposed secularisation while addressing modern Jewish public life.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee
bio: Formed in New York in 1914 to coordinate relief for Jews affected by the First World War, the Joint became a leading international Jewish humanitarian and welfare organisation.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Hebrew University of Jerusalem
bio: Formally founded in 1918 and opened in 1925, the Hebrew University became a central institution of Jewish scholarship, science and higher education.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Porat Yosef Yeshiva
bio: Porat Yosef became the flagship Sephardic yeshiva of Jerusalem, educating generations of rabbis and communal leaders. Its Old City building was destroyed in 1948 and later rebuilt.
image_credit: Historic image hosted by Wikimedia Commons, public domain in Israel.

name: Mercaz HaRav Yeshiva
bio: Founded in Jerusalem in 1924, Mercaz HaRav became a formative institution of Religious Zionist Torah learning and trained many rabbis, educators and communal leaders.
image_credit: Shimon Levin, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

name: Kamenitz Yeshiva
bio: Kamenitz Yeshiva was founded in 1926 in Kamenets-Litovsk by Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz, a disciple of Rabbi Chaim of Brisk. It became renowned for its Brisker style of Talmudic analysis. The yeshiva flourished until it was destroyed during the Holocaust, though its traditions continued in Israel and America through its students.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Edgware United Synagogue
bio: United Synagogue of Edgware
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Gateshead Talmudical College
bio: Founded in 1929, Gateshead Yeshiva developed into one of Europe's most important postwar centres of traditional Talmudic study and the nucleus of a wider Torah educational community.
image_credit: Andy Williamson, Newcastle University DECTE Picture Archive, CC BY.

name: Jewish Agency for Israel
bio: Constituted in 1929 from earlier Zionist institutions, the Jewish Agency coordinated immigration, settlement and political representation before statehood and later supported aliyah and Jewish connections with Israel.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Chachmei Lublin Yeshiva
bio: Founded in 1930 in Lublin, Poland, by Rabbi Meir Shapiro, Chachmei Lublin became a world-famous yeshiva and the birthplace of the Daf Yomi program. It was seized by the Nazis in 1939 and its library plundered. Today the restored building serves as a heritage site.
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Ner Israel Rabbinical College
bio: Founded in Baltimore in 1933, Ner Israel developed into one of the leading American Lithuanian-style yeshivot and a centre for rabbinical education.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Finchley United Synagogue
bio: United Synagogue in Finchley, also known as Kinloss
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: World Jewish Congress
bio: Founded in Geneva in 1936, the World Jewish Congress became an international federation representing Jewish communities and advocating for Jewish rights and security.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: 770 Eastern Parkway
bio: Acquired by Chabad-Lubavitch in 1940, 770 Eastern Parkway became the movement's world headquarters, central synagogue and a globally recognised symbol of Chabad.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Brisk Yeshiva, Jerusalem
bio: Established in Jerusalem by the Brisk rabbinic dynasty after its flight from Europe, the yeshiva became an influential centre for the analytical Brisker method of Talmud study.
image_credit: Yoninah, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

name: Beth Medrash Govoha
bio: Founded in Lakewood in 1943, Beth Medrash Govoha grew from a small wartime yeshiva into one of the world's largest centres of advanced Talmudic study and a major influence on Orthodox Jewish life in North America.
image_credit: Beth Medrash Govoha Archives, Wikimedia Commons.

name: Yeshurun Federation Synagogue
bio: Federation synagogue in Edgware
image_credit: Online archival or institutional image; follow the source page for attribution.

name: Yad Vashem
bio: Established by Israeli law in 1953, Yad Vashem is Israel's official memorial authority for the victims of the Holocaust, combining commemoration, documentation, research and education.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Kerem B'Yavneh
bio: Founded in 1954, Kerem B'Yavneh became the first hesder yeshiva, combining advanced Torah study with service in the Israel Defense Forces.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Bar-Ilan University
bio: Opened in 1955, Bar-Ilan University was created to combine academic research and higher education with a Jewish religious and cultural orientation.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Yeshivat Sha'alvim
bio: Founded in 1961 at Kibbutz Sha'alvim, this hesder yeshiva became a major centre of Religious Zionist Torah learning and teacher training.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Yeshivat HaKotel
bio: Founded after the reunification of Jerusalem in 1967, Yeshivat HaKotel became a prominent hesder yeshiva overlooking the Western Wall and a major institution of Religious Zionist education.
image_credit: Mattman090, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

name: Yeshivat Har Etzion
bio: Founded in 1968, Yeshivat Har Etzion became one of the most influential hesder yeshivot, known for rigorous Talmud study and intellectually open Religious Zionist thought.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Ohr Somayach, Jerusalem
bio: Founded in Jerusalem in 1970, Ohr Somayach became an international yeshiva network specialising in intensive Jewish learning for men with limited prior formal Torah education.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Aish HaTorah
bio: Founded in Jerusalem in 1974, Aish HaTorah developed into a global Jewish educational and outreach organisation centred on its Old City yeshiva overlooking the Western Wall.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Simon Wiesenthal Center
bio: Founded in Los Angeles in 1977, the Simon Wiesenthal Center developed as a Jewish human-rights organisation addressing antisemitism, Holocaust memory and contemporary hate.
image_credit: Online image; attribution and licence are available from the cited source or image file page.

name: Belz Great Synagogue
bio: Dedicated in 2000, the Belz Great Synagogue in Jerusalem is the monumental world centre of Belz Hasidism and consciously recalls the dynasty's destroyed synagogue in Belz, Galicia.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Ohel Jakob Synagogue, Munich
bio: Opened in 2006, Munich's Ohel Jakob Synagogue anchors the city's new Jewish Centre and symbolises the renewal of Jewish communal life in Bavaria after the Holocaust.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons; see file page for author and licence.

name: Ben Ezra Synagogue
bio: A historic synagogue in Old Cairo, closely associated with the Cairo Geniza, whose manuscripts transformed the study of medieval Jewish history. The present structure largely reflects nineteenth-century rebuilding on a much older site.
image_credit: Faris knight, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
